title: MGPO: Manifold-Guided Diffusion Alignment for Task-Aware Dataset Distillation

paper.title: MGPO: Manifold-Guided Diffusion Alignment for Task-Aware Dataset Distillation
paper.abstract:
Abstract Diffusion-based dataset distillation (DD) suffers from a fundamental
objective mismatch: likelihood-driven diffusion models prioritize density
approximation over the discriminative decision boundaries required for
downstream tasks. Beyond semantic mismatch, relying solely on
density also leads to geometric coverage loss, where generated samples collapse
into a few high-density modes and fail to cover the manifold’s structural
diversity. We propose Manifold-Guided Policy Optimization ( MGPO ),
which reformulates DD as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem
and achieves Dual-Space Alignment via a pixel-space discriminative
reward and a latent-space geometric reward guided by a class-wise Minimum
Spanning Tree (MST). The discriminative reward enforces class
separability, while the MST-based geometric reward encourages generated latents to cover a sparse geometric skeleton of each class, jointly addressing both failure
modes. We further provide an idealized analysis that motivates the MST-based reward, including a Hausdorff approximation bound and a subsampling bound
independent of the dataset size. The reward-modular design extends to structured tasks such as object detection and segmentation by substituting the frozen task reward model.
Extensive experiments show MGPO consistently outperforms existing methods,
including a +8.0% mIoU gain on segmentation under low-budget settings.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Dataset distillation (DD) ( Wang et al., 2018 ) has emerged as a critical technique in large-scale machine learning, aiming to synthesize a small, representative subset of data from a massive original dataset. Recently, generative models, particularly diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) , have emerged as effective backbones for this task. By leveraging powerful generative priors, diffusion models can effectively capture the complex underlying distribution of the source data to synthesize diverse and high-fidelity images. Unlike traditional gradient-matching ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) or trajectory-matching ( Cazenavette et al., 2022 ) approaches, which often struggle with optimization stability and limited sample diversity, these generative frameworks naturally overcome such bottlenecks. Consequently, diffusion-based methods have established state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in dataset distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Chan-Santiago et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025 ) , offering superior results within limited computational budgets. Despite recent advances, diffusion-based dataset distillation under extremely low-budget settings faces two distinct challenges. First, a semantic objective mismatch : likelihood-driven diffusion models prioritize pixel-level density approximation over the discriminative features required by downstream tasks ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Karczewski et al., 2025 ) . Second, a geometric coverage loss : relying solely on density or naive classifier guidance often leads to mode collapse, failing to capture the complex geometric manifold structure and structural diversity of each class in the original data distribution. Consequently, generated samples may exhibit high perceptual fidelity yet fail to effectively represent the dataset. These challenges show that diffusion-based distillation must transcend perceptual fidelity by resolving both issues at the same time. An effective distilled dataset requires two orthogonal properties: semantic discriminability, which pushes samples toward highly separable regions to better serve downstream tasks; and geometric preservation, which spreads samples along a sparse geometric skeleton of each class to maintain structural diversity and prevent mode collapse ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . Following these principles, we propose Manifold-Guided Policy Optimization ( MGPO ), a framework that reformulates diffusion-based dataset distillation as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem. Our core contribution is a Dual-Space Alignment strategy that addresses both challenges in their respective domains. We design a pixel-space discriminative reward to enforce class separability, alongside a latent-space geometric reward guided by a class-wise Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) to encourage geometric coverage. Crucially, MGPO utilizes a decoupled group-wise policy optimization strategy to internalize these heterogeneous, non-differentiable rewards directly into the diffusion weights. This RL formulation eliminates the need for expensive inference-time guidance, ensuring highly efficient sampling while harmonizing semantics and geometry. We further provide an idealized analysis showing that, under smoothness and reach assumptions, a Euclidean MST δ \delta -approximates the class manifold in Hausdorff distance with δ 2 / τ \delta^{2}/\tau tightness in the backward direction. This analysis motivates the distance term of the geometric reward; the implemented reward is evaluated empirically. Beyond classification, the flexibility of our RL formulation unlocks a new reward-modular paradigm for dataset distillation. While the MST-based geometric prior is inherently task-agnostic, the outer framework can be adapted to complex downstream tasks, such as object detection and segmentation, by substituting the pixel-space reward model. In such scenarios, the same frozen task model provides the reward during fine-tuning and pseudo-annotates the class-conditioned generated images afterwards, without modifying the core generative architecture. Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that MGPO consistently outperforms existing SOTA approaches. For instance, under representative low-budget settings, our method achieves 18.3 mIoU on segmentation tasks, surpassing the strongest baseline by +8.0 mIoU. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reformulate diffusion-based dataset distillation as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem, internalizing task-specific rewards directly into the diffusion weights and eliminating inference-time guidance overhead. • We design a dual-space reward with a pixel-level discriminative term and a latent-level MST geometric term, addressing the semantic mismatch and geometric coverage loss. • We provide an idealized analysis motivating the MST-based reward: under smoothness and reach assumptions, (i) a Euclidean MST approximates the class manifold in Hausdorff distance, and (ii) a subsampled MST admits a bound independent of the dataset size. • Extensive experiments show MGPO achieves SOTA performance on standard classification benchmarks and extends to other complex structured tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. Figure 2: Overview of the proposed MGPO framework. (a) Pixel Reward ( r disc r_{\text{disc}} ) is computed from downstream objectives such as classification, detection, and segmentation, encouraging semantic correctness and task consistency. (b) MST Reward ( r geo r_{\text{geo}} ) is constructed in latent space. Real dataset features are encoded by encoder and projected via PCA to obtain a structured latent representation. A kNN graph is built to approximate local neighborhood structure, followed by a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) to capture the global manifold topology. The generated latent samples are aligned with this manifold structure, promoting both representativeness and structural consistency.

sections.heading: 2.1 Diffusion Models for Dataset Distillation
sections.text: Recent work has explored diffusion models as powerful generative backbones for DD. Minimax ( Gu et al., 2024 ) fine-tunes pre-trained diffusion models under a minimax objective to balance sample representativeness and diversity. D 4 M ( Su et al., 2024 ) incorporates text-to-image diffusion with prototype learning to improve intra-class consistency. D3HR ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) addresses distribution mismatch via DDIM inversion ( Song et al., 2020 ) and group-wise sampling, aligning generated and real data distributions. CaO2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) performs inference-time latent optimization to reduce feature level inconsistencies, while DDVLCP ( Zou et al., 2025 ) leverages vision–language prototypes to enhance semantic coherence. Despite their success, diffusion-based approaches are inherently likelihood-centric, concentrating samples in high-density regions, which preserves perceptual fidelity but neglects boundary and hard examples essential for discriminative training. Most related to our work, ManifoldGD ( Roy et al., 2026 ) explores manifold structure for diffusion-based distillation, but relies on inference-time guidance without formal geometric guarantees. In contrast, MGPO internalizes geometric constraints into the diffusion policy via RL, with an idealized Hausdorff analysis motivating the MST-based reward, while simultaneously resolving the semantic objective mismatch through dual-space alignment.

sections.heading: 2.2 Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Models
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has recently been introduced to align diffusion and flow-based generative models with task-level objectives beyond likelihood-based training. A representative approach is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which stabilizes policy updates by comparing relative rewards within groups of sampled trajectories. Subsequent works extend GRPO to generative settings. Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) adapts it to diffusion and flow matching models, while Temp-Flow-GRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) introduces time-dependent credit assignment. Mix-GRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) combines multiple sampling dynamics, and structured variants such as Branch-GRPO ( Li et al., 2025 ) and Dance-GRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) improve scalability through branching and group-wise rollouts. However, existing methods focus primarily on generative quality or preference alignment. In contrast, we leverage reinforcement learning to directly optimize downstream discriminative objectives. More related works see Appendix B.1

sections.heading: 3.1 Dataset Distillation
sections.text: Dataset distillation aims to synthesize a small and compact dataset 𝒮 = { ( x ~ i , y ~ i ) } i = 1 N S \mathcal{S}=\{(\tilde{x}_{i},\tilde{y}_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{S}} that preserves the essential training information of a large-scale real dataset 𝒯 = { ( x i , y i ) } i = 1 N T , \mathcal{T}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N_{T}}, where x i x_{i} denotes an input sample (e.g., an image), y i y_{i} its corresponding label, and N S ≪ N T N_{S}\ll N_{T} . The goal of dataset distillation is to enable models trained on 𝒮 \mathcal{S} to achieve performance comparable to those trained on 𝒯 \mathcal{T} , while significantly reducing storage and computational costs.

sections.heading: 4 Method
sections.text: To bridge the gap between likelihood driven diffusion generation and discriminative downstream tasks, MGPO internalizes dual space task objectives into the diffusion backbone via RL.

sections.heading: 4.1 Dual-Space Reward Design

The discriminative reward encourages semantic separability in pixel space, while the geometric reward encourages coverage of class-level geometric structure in latent space. sections.heading: 4.2 MGPO : Manifold-Guided Policy Optimization
sections.text: We formulate diffusion-based dataset distillation as a sequential decision process (see Appendix A.1 ), where the diffusion model acts as a stochastic policy that gradually transforms Gaussian noise into a synthetic sample. At each timestep, the policy π θ ​ ( z t − 1 ∣ z t , c ) \pi_{\theta}(z_{t-1}\mid z_{t},c) predicts the reverse diffusion transition conditioned on the class label c c . Following the generalized DDIM formulation introduced in Sec. 3.2 , we set η = 1 \eta=1 during policy optimization to introduce stochasticity into the sampling process. This injected stochasticity is vital as it enables the policy to explore a broader range within latent space, while task-driven rewards guide the trajectories toward regions that are both discriminative and geometrically structured. sections.heading: 4.3 Reward-Modular Extension to Structured Tasks
sections.text: While the geometric reward r geo r_{\mathrm{geo}} in Section 4.1 is task-agnostic, structured tasks such as object detection and segmentation require pixel-space rewards that capture spatial, in addition to semantic, correctness. The modular design of MGPO allows substituting r disc r_{\mathrm{disc}} with such task-specific rewards while keeping the policy optimization, geometric reward, and overall training pipeline unchanged. We illustrate this with two examples; each task still requires a task-appropriate reward design, but the burden is reduced from modifying the framework to specifying a scalar reward signal. Object Detection. To encourage clear spatial boundaries without composite losses, we derive the reward from a pretrained detector. For an image x ~ 0 \tilde{x}_{0} conditioned on class c c , we apply Non-Maximum Suppression to filter redundant predictions, and define the reward as the maximum remaining confidence score for class c c : r det ​ ( x ~ 0 , c ) = max ⁡ ( 𝒮 c ​ ( x ~ 0 ) ) , r_{\mathrm{det}}(\tilde{x}_{0},c)=\max\bigl(\mathcal{S}_{c}(\tilde{x}_{0})\bigr), (9) where 𝒮 c ​ ( x ~ 0 ) \mathcal{S}_{c}(\tilde{x}_{0}) denotes the set of post-NMS confidence scores. Image Segmentation. Instead of relying on predefined mask annotations, we extract the spatial probability map from a pre-trained segmentation network. To prevent reward hacking via isolated high-confidence pixels, we average the top- K K pixel confidences for class c c : r seg ​ ( x ~ 0 , c ) = 1 K ​ ∑ k = 1 K TopK ​ ( 𝒫 c ​ ( x ~ 0 ) ) k , r_{\mathrm{seg}}(\tilde{x}_{0},c)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\mathrm{TopK}\bigl(\mathcal{P}_{c}(\tilde{x}_{0})\bigr)_{k}, (10) where 𝒫 c ​ ( x ~ 0 ) \mathcal{P}_{c}(\tilde{x}_{0}) is the flattened probability map. The hyperparameter K K enforces a minimum expected pixel area (analysis in Appendix). In both cases, the reward depends only on the prompted class c c . Spatial annotations are obtained by class-conditioned image generation followed by pseudo-annotation with the same frozen task model. For detection, we keep the post-NMS predictions of class c c (score threshold 0.05, IoU threshold 0.5) as boxes. For segmentation, we keep the pixels whose argmax prediction is c c as the mask; the Top- K K operation in Eq. ( 10 ) only computes the scalar reward. Images without a valid class- c c prediction are kept with empty annotations (detection) or an all-background mask (segmentation). The current formulation therefore does not model multi-class co-occurrence or inter-class relations (see Appendix F ). This reward-modular design allows MGPO to extend to new structured tasks through reward specification rather than architectural modification, though designing an effective reward for each task remains a non-trivial step (see Appendix C for further design considerations).

sections.heading: 5.1 Experimental Setup
sections.text: Generative Backbone. For classification experiments, we adopt a pretrained DiT-XL/2 ( Peebles & Xie, 2022 ) as the generative backbone and fine-tune it using DiffFit ( Xie et al., 2023 ) , all synthetic images are generated at a resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 . For detection and segmentation, we follow the experimental protocol of UniDD ( Qi et al., 2025 ) and employ Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the generative backbone to synthesize labeled images with structured annotations. Implementation Details. For classification, student networks are trained from scratch for 300 epochs using SGD with cosine learning-rate decay. For downstream tasks, we use Faster R-CNN ( Ren et al., 2016 ) with a ResNet-50 backbone for object detection and LR-ASPP with a MobileNetV3 ( Howard et al., 2019 ) backbone for semantic segmentation, with standard pretrained backbone weights. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB). To ensure statistical reliability, each synthetic dataset is generated three times and each downstream model is trained with three random seeds; we report mean ± \pm standard deviation. More details see Appendix C . Baselines. For classification, we compare against representative optimization-based and diffusion-based dataset distillation methods, including DM ( Zhao & Bilen, 2023 ) , IDC ( Kim et al., 2022 ) , SRe 2 L ( Yin et al., 2023 ) , RDED ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , Minimax ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , D 4 M ( Su et al., 2024 ) , DDVLCP ( Zou et al., 2025 ) , CaO2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and ManifoldGD ( Roy et al., 2026 ) . For segmentation and object detection, we primarily compare with UniDD ( Qi et al., 2025 ) , a recent universal dataset distillation framework. Since diffusion-based distillation for structured outputs remains relatively underexplored, we additionally include coreset selection baselines (Random, Uniform, K-Center ( Sener & Savarese, 2018 ) , and Herding ( Welling, 2009 ) ). Evaluation Protocol. For classification, we evaluate ConvNet-6, ResNetAP-10, and ResNet-18 trained from scratch. For segmentation and object detection, we follow standard training recipes with pretrained backbones as described above. Following prior works, we report the better performance between hard-label and soft-label supervision.

sections.heading: 6 Conclusion
sections.text: In this paper, we proposed MGPO , a reward driven RL framework that resolves the fundamental objective mismatch in diffusion-based dataset distillation. By integrating pixel level discriminative and latent level geometric rewards, MGPO effectively aligns the generative process with downstream tasks. Furthermore, our plug-and-play reward design enables the framework to extend beyond standard classification to complex downstream tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. Extensive experiments show that MGPO achieves state of the art performance across multiple classification benchmarks and successfully reaches state of the art on detection and segmentation tasks.

sections.heading: Ethics Statement
sections.text: This work does not involve human subjects, user studies, or the collection of new data. All experiments use publicly available benchmarks (ImageNet-1K and its subsets ImageWoof, ImageNette, and ImageIDC; PASCAL VOC 2012; MS-COCO), used under their respective licenses and terms of use; we do not redistribute the original images. Some of these datasets contain images of people collected from the web, and the synthesized distilled datasets may therefore reflect content and biases present in the source data. In addition, because MGPO optimizes the generator with frozen pretrained reward models (classifier, detector, or segmentation network), any biases in these reward models may be internalized and amplified in the distilled data; we discuss this risk and recommend auditing reward models before deployment in Appendix F . We do not foresee direct harmful applications beyond those common to generative models and dataset compression. The authors declare no conflicts of interest or sponsorship that could have influenced this work.

sections.heading: Reproducibility Statement
sections.text: We have made the following efforts to ensure reproducibility. The full method is described in Section 4 , including the DDIM sampling formulation (Section 3.2 ), the reward definitions (Section 4.1 ), and the complete training procedure (Algorithm 1 ). The MST construction is given in Algorithm 2 , with all preprocessing steps and hyperparameters (e.g., k k -NN size, PCA dimension, number of sampled latents per class) detailed in Appendix C.1 ; the latent geometric reward and the pixel-space rewards for classification, detection, and segmentation are specified in Appendices C.2 and C.3 (Algorithms 3 and 4 ). Experimental settings, including backbones, student architectures, training schedules, evaluation protocols, and the number of runs and random seeds, are given in Section 5.1 , and hyperparameter sensitivity analyses are reported in Section 5.4 and Appendix D . For the theoretical results, all assumptions are stated explicitly and complete proofs are provided in Appendices A.1 , A.2 , and A.3 . All datasets are publicly available. The source code will be released upon acceptance.

sections.heading: B.1 Optimization-Based Dataset Distillation
sections.text: Dataset distillation was originally introduced as a meta-learning problem that directly optimizes a small set of synthetic examples such that models trained on them achieve comparable performance to training on the full dataset ( Wang et al., 2018 ) . A dominant line of follow-up work formulates distillation as bi-level optimization, where the outer loop updates synthetic data and the inner loop trains a network on these synthetic samples ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) . Subsequent studies reduce accumulative error in optimization process by matching training trajectory. Later, SRe 2 L ( Yin et al., 2023 ) series of work further unleashed the ability of decoupling the distillation process by squeeze and recover approach. Besides, an alternative line of works matches higher-level statistics such as distribution or feature in representation space to avoid expensive unrolling, improving efficiency while sometimes sacrificing fidelity of training dynamics. Nevertheless, these optimization-based methods often suffer from heavy compute or memory overhead due to unrolling, sensitivity to architecture choices, and difficulties in scaling to higher resolutions or large numbers of classes.

sections.heading: B.2 Diffusion Models for Dataset Distillation
sections.text: Recent advances have explored diffusion models as powerful generative backbones for dataset distillation, enabling the synthesis of compact yet highly representative datasets. As a pioneering work, Minimax Diffusion ( Gu et al., 2024 ) leverages pre-trained diffusion models and further fine-tunes them under a minimax criteria to jointly enhance sample representativeness and diversity. Building upon this idea, D 4 M ( Su et al., 2024 ) incorporates pre-trained text-to-image diffusion models with prototype learning, clustering latent features to learn category prototypes and thereby improving intra-class consistency and visual fidelity. To mitigate distribution mismatch and stochasticity in latent sampling, D3HR ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) proposes a domain mapping framework that applies DDIM inversion ( Song et al., 2020 ) to project VAE latents into a Gaussian space with improved normality, combined with a group-based sampling strategy to better align the generated data distribution with the real one. More recently, CaO2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) rectifies feature and class level inconsistencies by inference time latent optimization. DDVLCP ( Zou et al., 2025 ) extends diffusion-based distillation to the vision–language setting by constructing paired image–text prototypes using large language models, which effectively enhances semantic coherence and reduces artifacts such as missing or illogical objects. Despite their success, diffusion-based approaches are inherently likelihood-centric, concentrating samples in high-density regions, which preserves perceptual fidelity but neglects boundary and hard examples essential for discriminative training.

sections.heading: B.3 Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion models
sections.text: Reinforcement learning has recently been adopted to align diffusion and flow based generative models with task level objectives that are difficult to encode through likelihood based training alone. A representative line of work builds upon Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which updates generative policies by comparing relative rewards within groups of sampled trajectories, enabling stable optimization without explicit value function estimation. Following the introduction of GRPO, several variants have been proposed to adapt it to different generative settings. Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) extends group relative optimization to diffusion and flow matching models by introducing controlled stochasticity into the sampling process. Temporal variants such as Temp-Flow-GRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) further incorporate time dependent credit assignment to emphasize critical denoising stages. Mix-GRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) combines multiple sampling dynamics within a unified optimization framework to balance exploration and efficiency. More recently, structured rollout strategies such as Branch-GRPO ( Li et al., 2025 ) and Dance-GRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) have been proposed to improve scalability and stability through branching trajectories and group wise reward aggregation. Despite these advances, existing GRPO-based methods primarily focus on improving generative quality or preference alignment. In contrast, our work leverages reinforcement learning to explicitly incorporate downstream discriminative objectives into the diffusion generation process, addressing the objective mismatch between likelihood-driven diffusion models and dataset distillation for classification.

sections.heading: C.1 MST Construction Details
sections.text: The class-wise MST skeleton is pre-computed once before MGPO fine-tuning. For each class c c , we sample up to N c N_{c} real images from the training set. All images are resized to 256 × 256 256\times 256 , center-cropped, converted to tensors, and normalized to the range [ − 1 , 1 ] [-1,1] . Each image is then encoded by a frozen Stable Diffusion VAE encoder. We use the mean of the encoder posterior as the latent representation and divide it by the standard latent scaling factor 0.18215 0.18215 . The resulting latent tensor is flattened into a vector. Stacking all vectors from class c c produces a latent matrix Z ∈ ℝ N × D , Z\in\mathbb{R}^{N\times D}, where N N is the number of collected samples and D D is the flattened latent dimension. Class-wise PCA normalization. To obtain a compact and numerically stable embedding space, we perform PCA on the centered latent matrix. Let μ c = 1 N ​ ∑ i = 1 N z i \mu_{c}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}z_{i} be the class mean and define the centered matrix Z c = Z − μ c . Z_{c}=Z-\mu_{c}. We compute a low-rank PCA decomposition of Z c Z_{c} and retain the top d d principal components. Let V ∈ ℝ D × d V\in\mathbb{R}^{D\times d} denote the projection matrix and S ∈ ℝ d S\in\mathbb{R}^{d} the singular values. To avoid numerical instability, singular values are lower-bounded by a small constant ε \varepsilon . Each latent vector z z is then projected into a normalized embedding space by u = g c ​ ( z ) = ( z − μ c ) ​ V ​ diag ⁡ ( S ) − 1 . u=g_{c}(z)=(z-\mu_{c})V\operatorname{diag}(S)^{-1}. This transformation simultaneously performs dimensionality reduction and whitening, making distances more comparable across directions. In our implementation, the PCA dimension is set to d = 128 d=128 . Sparse k k NN graph construction. After obtaining the normalized embeddings { u i } i = 1 N \{u_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} , we construct a sparse k k -nearest-neighbor graph in the embedding space. For each node u i u_{i} , we identify its k k nearest neighbors according to Euclidean distance. An adjacency matrix A A is then constructed where A i ​ j = { ‖ u i − u j ‖ 2 , if ​ u j ​ is among the ​ k ​ nearest neighbors of ​ u i , + ∞ , otherwise . A_{ij}=\begin{cases}\|u_{i}-u_{j}\|_{2},&\text{if }u_{j}\text{ is among the }k\text{ nearest neighbors of }u_{i},\\ +\infty,&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases} The graph is symmetrized by assigning the same edge weight to both A i ​ j A_{ij} and A j ​ i A_{ji} once either direction is observed. This sparse construction significantly reduces graph density and improves scalability. In practice, we use k = 10 k=10 . Minimum spanning tree extraction. Given the sparse adjacency matrix, we compute the minimum spanning tree using a standard graph solver. The resulting tree is represented as an edge set ℰ c = { ( i , j ) } , \mathcal{E}_{c}=\{(i,j)\}, which connects all nodes while minimizing the total edge weight. Ideally, a spanning tree over N N nodes contains N − 1 N-1 edges. The extracted tree therefore provides a sparse skeleton of the class manifold that preserves global connectivity while avoiding redundant edges. Saved statistics. For each class, we store the PCA mean μ c \mu_{c} , the projection matrix V V , the singular values S S , the normalized node embeddings, and the MST edge list. These quantities define both the class-wise tree 𝒯 c \mathcal{T}_{c} and the projection function g c ​ ( ⋅ ) g_{c}(\cdot) used during MGPO training. When a generated latent z 0 z_{0} is obtained at the end of the diffusion trajectory, it is projected using the same transformation g c ​ ( ⋅ ) g_{c}(\cdot) and evaluated according to its geometric relation to the nearest edge of the corresponding MST skeleton.

Specifically, we analyze the parameters involved in the construction of the MST that models the latent geometric structure. By varying these parameters while keeping other settings fixed, we evaluate the robustness of our framework and examine how they influence the quality of the generated synthetic data and the downstream performance (Figure 5 ). Overall, MGPO exhibits stable performance across a broad range of hyperparameter settings. sections.heading: Limitations.
sections.text: While MGPO establishes an efficient and adaptable paradigm for task aware dataset distillation, it still possesses certain limitations. First, from a theoretical perspective, as discussed in remark 12 , the direction component of the geometric reward relies on local tangent approximations which may exhibit fluctuations on high intrinsic dimension manifolds. Second, although MGPO eliminates the computational bottleneck of inference time guidance, the reinforcement learning policy optimization phase introduces additional offline training overhead compared to purely training free selection methods. Finally, scaling the class wise MST construction to datasets with millions of categories might require more advanced hierarchical clustering algorithms to maintain strict scalability.

sections.heading: Broader Societal Impacts.
sections.text: Our research presents significant positive societal impacts by heavily compressing the data required to train deep learning models. This inherently reduces the carbon footprint and energy consumption associated with large scale model training, democratizing artificial intelligence by allowing researchers with limited computational resources to train state of the art models. However, as a potential negative impact, if the pre-trained reward models (such as the proxy classifier or detector) contain inherent biases regarding demographic attributes, the policy optimization process might internalize and amplify these biases within the distilled dataset. Therefore, practitioners must ensure that the reward models used for distillation are thoroughly audited for fairness and equity prior to deployment in sensitive applications.

Abstract Diffusion-based dataset distillation (DD) suffers from a fundamental objective mismatch: likelihood-driven diffusion models prioritize density approximation over the discriminative decision boundaries required for downstream tasks. Beyond semantic mismatch, relying solely on density also leads to geometric coverage loss, where generated samples collapse into a few high-density modes and fail to cover the manifold’s structural diversity. We propose Manifold-Guided Policy Optimization ( MGPO ), which reformulates DD as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem and achieves Dual-Space Alignment via a pixel-space discriminative reward and a latent-space geometric reward guided by a class-wise Minimum Spanning Tree (MST). The discriminative reward enforces class separability, while the MST-based geometric reward encourages generated latents to cover a sparse geometric skeleton of each class, jointly addressing both failure modes. We further provide an idealized analysis that motivates the MST-based reward, including a Hausdorff approximation bound and a subsampling bound independent of the dataset size. The reward-modular design extends to structured tasks such as object detection and segmentation by substituting the frozen task reward model. Extensive experiments show MGPO consistently outperforms existing methods, including a +8.0% mIoU gain on segmentation under low-budget settings. Figure 1: t-SNE of latent distributions on ImageWoof. Blue density: real data; orange dots: Minimax Diffusion; red dots: MGPO (ours); red stars with green edges: class-wise MST skeleton. MGPO covers a broader area along the MST skeleton, indicating improved manifold coverage. 1 Introduction Dataset distillation (DD) ( Wang et al., 2018 ) has emerged as a critical technique in large-scale machine learning, aiming to synthesize a small, representative subset of data from a massive original dataset. Recently, generative models, particularly diffusion models ( Ho et al., 2020 ; Song et al., 2020 ) , have emerged as effective backbones for this task. By leveraging powerful generative priors, diffusion models can effectively capture the complex underlying distribution of the source data to synthesize diverse and high-fidelity images. Unlike traditional gradient-matching ( Zhao et al., 2020 ) or trajectory-matching ( Cazenavette et al., 2022 ) approaches, which often struggle with optimization stability and limited sample diversity, these generative frameworks naturally overcome such bottlenecks. Consequently, diffusion-based methods have established state-of-the-art (SOTA) performance in dataset distillation ( Gu et al., 2024 ; Su et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025 ; Chan-Santiago et al., 2025 ; Zou et al., 2025 ; Qi et al., 2025 ) , offering superior results within limited computational budgets. Despite recent advances, diffusion-based dataset distillation under extremely low-budget settings faces two distinct challenges. First, a semantic objective mismatch : likelihood-driven diffusion models prioritize pixel-level density approximation over the discriminative features required by downstream tasks ( Biroli et al., 2024 ; Ho et al., 2020 ; Karczewski et al., 2025 ) . Second, a geometric coverage loss : relying solely on density or naive classifier guidance often leads to mode collapse, failing to capture the complex geometric manifold structure and structural diversity of each class in the original data distribution. Consequently, generated samples may exhibit high perceptual fidelity yet fail to effectively represent the dataset. These challenges show that diffusion-based distillation must transcend perceptual fidelity by resolving both issues at the same time. An effective distilled dataset requires two orthogonal properties: semantic discriminability, which pushes samples toward highly separable regions to better serve downstream tasks; and geometric preservation, which spreads samples along a sparse geometric skeleton of each class to maintain structural diversity and prevent mode collapse ( Guo et al., 2024 ) . Following these principles, we propose Manifold-Guided Policy Optimization ( MGPO ), a framework that reformulates diffusion-based dataset distillation as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem. Our core contribution is a Dual-Space Alignment strategy that addresses both challenges in their respective domains. We design a pixel-space discriminative reward to enforce class separability, alongside a latent-space geometric reward guided by a class-wise Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) to encourage geometric coverage. Crucially, MGPO utilizes a decoupled group-wise policy optimization strategy to internalize these heterogeneous, non-differentiable rewards directly into the diffusion weights. This RL formulation eliminates the need for expensive inference-time guidance, ensuring highly efficient sampling while harmonizing semantics and geometry. We further provide an idealized analysis showing that, under smoothness and reach assumptions, a Euclidean MST δ \delta -approximates the class manifold in Hausdorff distance with δ 2 / τ \delta^{2}/\tau tightness in the backward direction. This analysis motivates the distance term of the geometric reward; the implemented reward is evaluated empirically. Beyond classification, the flexibility of our RL formulation unlocks a new reward-modular paradigm for dataset distillation. While the MST-based geometric prior is inherently task-agnostic, the outer framework can be adapted to complex downstream tasks, such as object detection and segmentation, by substituting the pixel-space reward model. In such scenarios, the same frozen task model provides the reward during fine-tuning and pseudo-annotates the class-conditioned generated images afterwards, without modifying the core generative architecture. Extensive empirical evaluations across multiple benchmarks demonstrate that MGPO consistently outperforms existing SOTA approaches. For instance, under representative low-budget settings, our method achieves 18.3 mIoU on segmentation tasks, surpassing the strongest baseline by +8.0 mIoU. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • We reformulate diffusion-based dataset distillation as a multi-objective reinforcement learning problem, internalizing task-specific rewards directly into the diffusion weights and eliminating inference-time guidance overhead. • We design a dual-space reward with a pixel-level discriminative term and a latent-level MST geometric term, addressing the semantic mismatch and geometric coverage loss. • We provide an idealized analysis motivating the MST-based reward: under smoothness and reach assumptions, (i) a Euclidean MST approximates the class manifold in Hausdorff distance, and (ii) a subsampled MST admits a bound independent of the dataset size. • Extensive experiments show MGPO achieves SOTA performance on standard classification benchmarks and extends to other complex structured tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. (b) MST Reward ( r geo r_{\text{geo}} ) is constructed in latent space. Real dataset features are encoded by encoder and projected via PCA to obtain a structured latent representation. A kNN graph is built to approximate local neighborhood structure, followed by a Minimum Spanning Tree (MST) to capture the global manifold topology. The generated latent samples are aligned with this manifold structure, promoting both representativeness and structural consistency. 2 Related Work 2.1 Diffusion Models for Dataset Distillation Recent work has explored diffusion models as powerful generative backbones for DD. Minimax ( Gu et al., 2024 ) fine-tunes pre-trained diffusion models under a minimax objective to balance sample representativeness and diversity. D 4 M ( Su et al., 2024 ) incorporates text-to-image diffusion with prototype learning to improve intra-class consistency. D3HR ( Zhao et al., 2025 ) addresses distribution mismatch via DDIM inversion ( Song et al., 2020 ) and group-wise sampling, aligning generated and real data distributions. CaO2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) performs inference-time latent optimization to reduce feature level inconsistencies, while DDVLCP ( Zou et al., 2025 ) leverages vision–language prototypes to enhance semantic coherence. Despite their success, diffusion-based approaches are inherently likelihood-centric, concentrating samples in high-density regions, which preserves perceptual fidelity but neglects boundary and hard examples essential for discriminative training. Most related to our work, ManifoldGD ( Roy et al., 2026 ) explores manifold structure for diffusion-based distillation, but relies on inference-time guidance without formal geometric guarantees. In contrast, MGPO internalizes geometric constraints into the diffusion policy via RL, with an idealized Hausdorff analysis motivating the MST-based reward, while simultaneously resolving the semantic objective mismatch through dual-space alignment. 2.2 Reinforcement Learning in Diffusion Models Reinforcement learning has recently been introduced to align diffusion and flow-based generative models with task-level objectives beyond likelihood-based training. A representative approach is Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) ( Shao et al., 2024 ) , which stabilizes policy updates by comparing relative rewards within groups of sampled trajectories. Subsequent works extend GRPO to generative settings. Flow-GRPO ( Liu et al., 2025 ) adapts it to diffusion and flow matching models, while Temp-Flow-GRPO ( He et al., 2025 ) introduces time-dependent credit assignment. Mix-GRPO ( Li et al., 2026 ) combines multiple sampling dynamics, and structured variants such as Branch-GRPO ( Li et al., 2025 ) and Dance-GRPO ( Xue et al., 2025 ) improve scalability through branching and group-wise rollouts. However, existing methods focus primarily on generative quality or preference alignment. In contrast, we leverage reinforcement learning to directly optimize downstream discriminative objectives. For classification experiments, we adopt a pretrained DiT-XL/2 ( Peebles & Xie, 2022 ) as the generative backbone and fine-tune it using DiffFit ( Xie et al., 2023 ) , all synthetic images are generated at a resolution of 256 × 256 256\times 256 . For detection and segmentation, we follow the experimental protocol of UniDD ( Qi et al., 2025 ) and employ Stable Diffusion v1.4 ( Rombach et al., 2022 ) as the generative backbone to synthesize labeled images with structured annotations. Implementation Details. For classification, student networks are trained from scratch for 300 epochs using SGD with cosine learning-rate decay. For downstream tasks, we use Faster R-CNN ( Ren et al., 2016 ) with a ResNet-50 backbone for object detection and LR-ASPP with a MobileNetV3 ( Howard et al., 2019 ) backbone for semantic segmentation, with standard pretrained backbone weights. All experiments are conducted on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU (80GB). To ensure statistical reliability, each synthetic dataset is generated three times and each downstream model is trained with three random seeds; we report mean ± \pm standard deviation. More details see Appendix C . Baselines. For classification, we compare against representative optimization-based and diffusion-based dataset distillation methods, including DM ( Zhao & Bilen, 2023 ) , IDC ( Kim et al., 2022 ) , SRe 2 L ( Yin et al., 2023 ) , RDED ( Sun et al., 2024 ) , Minimax ( Gu et al., 2024 ) , D 4 M ( Su et al., 2024 ) , DDVLCP ( Zou et al., 2025 ) , CaO2 ( Wang et al., 2025 ) , and ManifoldGD ( Roy et al., 2026 ) . For segmentation and object detection, we primarily compare with UniDD ( Qi et al., 2025 ) , a recent universal dataset distillation framework. Since diffusion-based distillation for structured outputs remains relatively underexplored, we additionally include coreset selection baselines (Random, Uniform, K-Center ( Sener & Savarese, 2018 ) , and Herding ( Welling, 2009 ) ). Evaluation Protocol. For classification, we evaluate ConvNet-6, ResNetAP-10, and ResNet-18 trained from scratch. For segmentation and object detection, we follow standard training recipes with pretrained backbones as described above. Figure 4: Ablation studies on key design choices of MGPO finetuning process. 6 Conclusion In this paper, we proposed MGPO , a reward driven RL framework that resolves the fundamental objective mismatch in diffusion-based dataset distillation. By integrating pixel level discriminative and latent level geometric rewards, MGPO effectively aligns the generative process with downstream tasks. Furthermore, our plug-and-play reward design enables the framework to extend beyond standard classification to complex downstream tasks like object detection and semantic segmentation. Extensive experiments show that MGPO achieves state of the art performance across multiple classification benchmarks and successfully reaches state of the art on detection and segmentation tasks.
